prompt: An account is disabled at 09:00. Its stateless JWT access token was issued at 08:30 and expires eight hours later. The API validates signature and claims, including exp, but does no credential revocation/account lookup. What exposure remains, and what reduces it without a per-request database lookup?

options.text: No exposure; disabling the account invalidates the JWT
options.explanation: A stateless JWT is verified purely by its signature and claims. The API never consults the account table, so disabling the account changes nothing until expiry.

options.text: Until 16:30. Shorten access tokens to ~10 minutes and use refresh tokens that are checked against the account on each refresh
options.explanation: Correct under the stated validation policy. Short access-token lifetimes reduce exposure to at most about ten minutes if refreshes check the current account state. A jti deny-list can enforce earlier token credential revocation, subject to propagation and cache delays.

options.text: Until 16:30. Switch from RS256 to HS256
options.explanation: Changing the signing algorithm doesn't affect lifetime or credential revocation. It would also make every verifier capable of forging tokens.

Issuing a new signing key alone does not invalidate tokens signed by a still-trusted old key. Removing the old verification key from every verifier can invalidate all tokens using it, with propagation/cache delays and broad disruption.

workedExample: A signature and expiry check do not consult the disabled account. Without another credential revocation mechanism the previously issued token remains usable until it expires. Shorter access-token lifetimes bound that exposure, while account checks at refresh stop further tokens being issued. Refresh checks do not revoke already-issued access tokens by themselves.
